support.exact_paragraph: The map $(x,y)\mapsto((x+y)/2,x-y)$ is an invertible linear map with absolute determinant $1$. The product of $a$, $u$, and $\overline u$ in the Weyl pairing is Schwartz in the transformed variables, so it is absolutely integrable. Fubini [F5] and change of variables [F8] give $$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a(q,\xi)u(q-r/2)\overline{u(q+r/2)}\,dq\,dr\,d\xi . $$ Applying [F8] to the reflection $y=-r$ turns the last two factors and the exponential into the defining integrand of $W_\epsilon[u]$; hence the pairing identity follows. [given, A1, F2, F5, F8, algebra]

The function $g(x,y):=u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}$ is Schwartz on $\mathbb R^{2d}$, because $(x,y)\mapsto(x+y/2,x-y/2)$ is invertible linear and products of Schwartz functions are Schwartz. Its full negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier transform $\widehat g(\eta,\zeta)$ is Schwartz by [F3]; applying inverse Fourier transformation in $\eta$ by [F4] gives the partial transform $\int e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\zeta}g(x,y)\,dy$, Schwartz jointly in $(x,\zeta)$. The desired partial transform with phase $e^{-iy\cdot\zeta'}$ is this function at $\zeta=\zeta'/(2\pi)$; frequency dilation preserves Schwartz space. Replacing $\zeta'$ by $\xi/\epsilon$ and multiplying by $(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}$ therefore gives $W_\epsilon[u]\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})\subset L^1$. Conjugating the defining integral and applying [F8] to the reflection $y\mapsto-y$ returns the same integral, so $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real. [given, A1, F1, F3, F4, F8, algebra]

Fix $x$ and set $f_x(y):=u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}$. The integrand $\widehat f_x$ is Schwartz and hence in $L^1$. Apply [F8] to the positive scaling $\eta\mapsto\xi=\epsilon\eta$, whose Jacobian is $\epsilon^d$, to obtain the substitution $\eta=\xi/\epsilon$ and $d\xi=\epsilon^d d\eta$. Write $\widehat f_x(\eta)=\int e^{-iy\cdot\eta}f_x(y)\,dy$, the rescaled negative-sign $2\pi$ transform. Then $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=(2\pi)^{-d}\int\widehat{f_x}(\eta)\,d\eta=f_x(0)=|u(x)|^2, $$ where the middle equality follows from [F4] at zero after the change from the library frequency $\eta/(2\pi)$ to $\eta$, also covered by [F8]. All integrals are absolutely convergent because $f_x,\widehat{f_x}\in\mathcal S$. [given, A1, F3, F4, F8, algebra]

For the momentum marginal, $u\in\mathcal S\subseteq L^1$, so the double integral in $x,y$ is absolutely integrable by Fubini [F5]. The affine change $(x,y)\mapsto(q,r)=(x+y/2,x-y/2)$ has absolute determinant $1$ and $q-r=y$; [F8] therefore gives $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{-i(q-r)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(q)\overline{u(r)}\,dq\,dr=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$ The last equality is the product of the scaled Fourier integral with its complex conjugate. [given, A1, F2, F5, F8, algebra]

To see that nonnegativity fails, set $v_\epsilon(x)=\sqrt{2/\epsilon}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/4}x e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}$. Substituting $x=\sqrt\epsilon\,s$ and applying [F6] at Gaussian parameter $1/4$ gives $\int e^{-s^2}ds=\sqrt\pi$; one integration by parts [F7] then gives $\int s^2e^{-s^2}ds=\sqrt\pi/2$, hence $\int x^2e^{-x^2/\epsilon}dx=\sqrt\pi\,\epsilon^{3/2}/2$ and $\|v_\epsilon\|_2=1$. At the origin, $$ W_\epsilon[v_\epsilon](0,0)=-(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}\frac{1}{2\epsilon\sqrt{\pi\epsilon}}\int y^2e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}\,dy=-\frac1{\pi\epsilon}<0. $$ Here the Gaussian second moment is obtained from [F6] at $\xi=0$ by one integration by parts [F7]. Thus $W_\epsilon[v_\epsilon]$ is a normalized Schwartz Wigner distribution with a negative value. [given, A1, F6, F7, algebra] ∎
